notes.meaning: Judah was the first tribe to receive its land by lot, matching the leadership role God promised to Judah through Jacob. Its territory lay in the far south of Canaan, reaching to the border of Edom and the dry desert of Zin. This large boundary showed how important Judah would be in Israel's future history.

Judah's southern boundary began at the south end of the Salt Sea, also known as the Dead Sea. It wound south past the Ascent of Akrabbim and Kadesh-barnea, and went out to the Mediterranean Sea by the Brook of Egypt. This line also served as the southern border for the entire Promised Land.
On the east, Judah's land was bordered by the full length of the Salt Sea up to where the Jordan River empties into it. The northern border began right at that northern bay of the sea.
The line went up into the hills past Beth-hoglah and north of Beth-arabah toward the Stone of Bohan. Bohan was a warrior from the tribe of Reuben, and his stone served as a well-known boundary mark.

The boundary climbed higher from the Valley of Achor, passing north toward Gilgal and past springs like En-shemesh and En-rogel. The Valley of Achor reminded Israel of Achan's sin, showing that obedience brings blessing while disobedience brings trouble.

The border moved along the Valley of Hinnom right next to the hill where the Jebusite city of Jerusalem stood. Because the boundary ran along this ridge, Jerusalem sat right between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. Later in Israel's history, this valley became notorious for idolatry, giving its name to the New Testament word for hell.

From the ridge west of Jerusalem, the border curved through the hills to Baalah, which was also named Kiriath-jearim. It then continued west past Beth-shemesh and Ekron, finally reaching the coast of the Mediterranean Sea. These careful lines marked off Judah's northern frontier before the land was given out.

The western border of Judah was the Mediterranean coastline, called the Great Sea. God set these clear limits for the clans of Judah so each family knew where their home was. Having assigned boundaries taught the people to live peacefully alongside their neighbors.

Joshua gave Caleb the city of Hebron, earlier called Kiriath-arba after a famous giant ancestor, just as the Lord had promised. Even though Joshua loved his old friend Caleb, he made sure this special gift followed God's direct command. God faithfully kept the promise He made to Caleb forty-five years earlier in the wilderness.

Caleb drove out the three Anakim chiefs—Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai—from the hill country of Hebron. These giants had terrified the other spies decades before, but Caleb trusted in God's power rather than his own strength. God gave him victory because he had whole-heartedly followed the Lord.

From Hebron, Caleb led an attack against Debir, which used to be called Kiriath-sepher, meaning the city of books or records. Debir was a strong and difficult fortress in the hills south of Hebron. Caleb wanted to clear out the remaining enemies so his tribe could live securely.

Caleb challenged the warriors by promising his daughter Acsah in marriage to whoever could conquer the fortified town of Debir. This offer was meant to encourage bold leadership and faith in the younger generation of Israel. In ancient times, fathers often chose husbands for their daughters, expecting them to agree to an honorable hero.

Caleb's nephew Othniel accepted the challenge, captured Debir, and received Acsah as his wife. This brave victory showed the courage that would later make Othniel Israel's first judge. Starting well in youth prepared him for a lifetime of serving God's people.

When Acsah was moving to her new home, she urged Othniel to ask her father for an additional field. As she came to Caleb, she got down from her donkey in humble respect, and Caleb asked what she wanted. Her action showed both high honor for her father and bold care for her future household.

Acsah asked her father for a gift of water springs because the land he gave her in the south was dry and parched. Caleb generously granted her request, giving her both upper and lower springs to water the surrounding fields. God's people are encouraged to bring their practical daily needs honestly and boldly before their loving Father.

This statement closes the description of Judah's borders and Caleb's inheritance, confirming the entire region as the lot given to Judah's clans. God provided an abundant, fertile territory to fulfill His ancient promise to the tribe.

The list of Judah's inheritance begins with the southernmost cities in the Negev desert along the border of Edom. These frontier towns had to be guarded faithfully by Judah to keep Israel safe from old enemies to the south.
